# A Text-to-SQL Benchmark for Official Statistics

[All reading notes](../reading-notes.md) · [Catalog entry](../README.md#locust)

**Full paper read · 2026-11-26**

[Original source](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.32646v1) · arXiv:2611.32646v1, 24 November 2026, 13 pages.

**Reading coverage:** Read Sections I–VII, acknowledgements and references, Tables I–X and all four figures. Checked the original PDF figures for graph structure, annotation workflow and results. There is no appendix in this version.

**Additional inspected sources:** [Pinned artifact and version-specific counts](https://github.com/lagewel001/LOCuST/blob/827adfc792ea19ea2a87e9964d417211b6723be9/README.md) · [Published selection scorer](https://github.com/lagewel001/LOCuST/blob/827adfc792ea19ea2a87e9964d417211b6723be9/evaluation/metrics/selection_metrics.py)

## Research question

An official-statistics question can identify its target numbers without specifying every column the answer should display. An exact comparison may punish a reasonable projection, while a measure-only check may miss an incorrect calculation.

## Method

LOCuST pairs English and Dutch questions with Statistics Netherlands tables and a graph connecting codes to concepts and units. Four Statistics Netherlands reviewers helped validate SQL-first examples. Retrieval, generation with supplied tables and end-to-end QA are separate tasks. The observation score pools overlap over measure and dimension-code sets and gives zero when no measure matches.

## Evaluation

The paper reports 2,559 questions and 2,241 tables across 22 domains. Questions in six domains are held out, with 308 English and 299 Dutch test items. Four generators are evaluated with supplied tables and with retrieved tables. Strict and lenient execution, numeric F1 and graph-grounded selection metrics capture different failure modes.

## What the results support

For generation with supplied tables, the authors report that 17–53% of questions per run receive perfect observation and numeric F1 but zero lenient execution accuracy. They illustrate how adding or omitting region, time and sector context changes the returned table. Conversely, only 76% of executable predictions with perfect observation F1 also attain perfect numeric F1.

## Limits and qualifications

A predicted set of codes can match despite a wrong range predicate, aggregation or join. The tested questions admit answers by construction, with unsupported requests and conflicting units discussed as future work. The paper’s counts differ from the repository README. The percentages describe model runs in this benchmark and do not count independently adjudicated valid interpretations.

## Relevance to reliable Text-to-SQL

Provides an adjacent benchmark and diagnostic scorer for the gap between a requested statistic and its displayed output. It has no scored clarification or abstention action.

## Checks against the paper

These are interpretations checked against the source, not verbatim quotations attributed to its authors.

| Claim or inference examined | Original evidence | Location | Assessment |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Does zero lenient execution accuracy always mean a wrong statistic? | One example returns the requested electricity quantity while the reference also projects descriptive fields. With the tables supplied, observation and numeric F1 can both be perfect while the full-cell comparison fails. | Sections III-D and V-A4, pp. 7–10 | Some execution discrepancies are consistent with underspecified presentation. The two F1 scores alone cannot certify correctness for each prediction. |
| Does a perfect observation score establish the calculation is right? | The score compares selected concepts and filters. Section V-B reports that 76% of executable predictions with perfect observation F1 have perfect numeric F1. A two-table task can earn partial credit from just one table. | Sections III-D2, V-A5 and V-B1, Tables V–VI | Use the score to identify which concepts the model selected. Check arithmetic and cross-table operations independently. |
| Can LOCuST compare refusal or clarification policies? | The authors explicitly exclude incompatible-unit aggregations and other unanswerable cases from the test set. Their three tasks use recorded question–SQL pairs and do not elicit replies from a user. | Sections III and VI | The benchmark can diagnose groundings and output conventions. It supplies no evaluation of appropriate refusal or successful dialogue. |
